titleEn: Praise the name of the LORD
progression: | G C | G D | Em C | G G |
intro: Twenty one verses of praise, framed by the same word at both ends: {{1.0}} at the opening and {{21.6}} at the close. Almost every line of this psalm is found somewhere else in the Bible, which is the first thing to know about it. Verse 7 stands nearly word for word in Jeremiah, verse 13 reuses the pairing of name and renown from Exodus 3, verse 14 is a line of Deuteronomy 32, and verses 15 to 18 are a compressed version of Psalm 115. For a learner it is the easiest praise psalm to read aloud, because it repeats structures deliberately: three imperatives in verse 1, the same relative clause opening verses 8 and 10, and a fixed four word pattern for each idol in verses 16 and 17 that breaks on purpose in the last line.

stichs.en: Halleluyah.
Praise the name of the LORD;
give praise, servants of the LORD,

verses.summary: Three imperatives before the psalm says anything at all about God, and the third one finally names its audience: servants, not the general public.

stichs.en: who stand in the house of the LORD,
in the courts of the house of our God.

verses.summary: The audience is located rather than described. Whoever happens to be standing in the courts is the choir this psalm is talking to.

stichs.en: Praise Yah, for the LORD is good;
sing to His name, for it is pleasant.

verses.summary: Two reasons are given for singing, and they are not the same kind of reason. The first is about God and the second is about the singing itself being pleasant to do.

stichs.en: For Yah chose Jacob for Himself,
Israel as His treasured possession.

verses.summary: Election stated flatly as a past fact, with the ancestor's two names used in the two halves so that the man and the nation are the same subject.

stichs.en: For I myself know that the LORD is great,
and our Lord is above all gods.

verses.summary: The speaker steps out of the chorus for one verse, with the pronoun written out for emphasis. Everything before this is command and everything after it is evidence.

stichs.en: All that the LORD wanted, He did,
in the heavens and on the earth, in the seas and all the deeps.

verses.summary: The thesis the next eight verses will demonstrate: what happens is what was wanted. The four locations are stacked from top to bottom to cover the whole world.

stichs.en: He raises clouds from the end of the earth,
He makes lightning for the rain,
He brings wind out of His storehouses.

verses.summary: Weather run as an administration. Clouds, lightning and wind are drawn from a store, which makes rain a matter of policy rather than of chance.

stichs.en: Who struck down the firstborn of Egypt,
from human to animal.

verses.summary: The move from nature to history happens with no seam. The same participial style that raised the clouds now strikes Egypt, as if both were weather.

stichs.en: He sent signs and wonders into your midst, Egypt,
against Pharaoh and against all his servants.

verses.summary: Egypt is suddenly addressed in the second person feminine, as countries are in Hebrew, as though it were standing in the room while the psalm lists what was done to it.

stichs.en: Who struck down many nations
and killed mighty kings:

verses.summary: The formula of verse 8 comes back to open the second historical panel. The subject is no longer the exodus but the approach to the land.

stichs.en: Sihon king of the Amorites,
and Og king of Bashan,
and all the kingdoms of Canaan.

verses.summary: Two named kings and then a whole region, which is the standard short form of the conquest. The next psalm uses the same list in the same order.

stichs.en: and gave their land as a possession,
a possession for Israel His people.

verses.summary: The point of the whole list. The key word is set down twice in a row so that the gift cannot be mistaken for a loan.

stichs.en: LORD, Your name is forever,
LORD, Your renown through every generation.

verses.summary: The historical section closes on the name rather than on the deeds, and the tense stops being past. The deeds were events; the name is a standing fact.

stichs.en: For the LORD will bring justice for His people
and relent concerning His servants.

verses.summary: The one verse in the psalm that looks forward, and it is not a threat: judging His people stands in parallel with having a change of heart about them.

stichs.en: The idols of the nations
are silver and gold, the work of human hands.

verses.summary: The pivot to the idols leads with the material. Silver and gold are the expensive part of the argument, and the answer to them is that they were still handled into shape.

stichs.en: They have a mouth and do not speak,
they have eyes and do not see,

verses.summary: The anatomy list begins. Each organ is granted and then cancelled in the same breath by the verb it cannot perform, four words at a time.

stichs.en: they have ears and do not listen,
and there is no breath at all in their mouth.

verses.summary: The list breaks its own pattern in the final line. Instead of a fourth organ with a verb attached, there is simply nothing coming out, which is the whole argument in one clause.

stichs.en: Their makers will become like them,
everyone who trusts in them.

verses.summary: The conclusion of the idol passage, and the only sentence in it about people. Worship is treated as something that works on the worshipper, not only on the object.

stichs.en: House of Israel, bless the LORD;
house of Aaron, bless the LORD;

verses.summary: The imperatives of verse 1 return, now handed out house by house, each clause built from the same three words with only the addressee changing.

stichs.en: House of Levi, bless the LORD;
you who fear the LORD, bless the LORD.

verses.summary: Levi is added to the roll, and then a fourth group with no lineage at all, defined only by what it fears. That is where the widening lands.

stichs.en: Blessed is the LORD from Zion,
who dwells in Jerusalem.
Halleluyah.

verses.summary: The blessing that was being handed out turns around and goes back, and the psalm closes on the same word it opened with.

pardes.body: Four movements inside one frame. Verses 1 to 4 call for praise and give the reason, which is election, stated as something already done. Verses 5 to 14 are the evidence, and they run in one continuous sweep from weather to history without marking the join: clouds and lightning, then Egypt, then Sihon and Og, then the land handed over, then the name that outlasts all of it. Verses 15 to 18 turn to the idols and argue by inventory, granting each part of the body and removing its function. Verses 19 to 21 pick the imperatives back up and hand them out by group. The frame is the word at {{1.0}} and again at {{21.6}}, so the psalm ends by saying its own first word. Notice what the argument in verses 15 to 18 actually is: not that the idols are weak but that they are inert, and that the people who made them are drifting toward the same condition.

This psalm is a mosaic, and reading it next to its sources is the fastest way into it. Verse 7 appears almost word for word in Jeremiah 10:13 and again at Jeremiah 51:16. Verse 13 reuses the pairing of name and memorial from Exodus 3:15, so {{13.4}} is not a synonym for name but the second half of a fixed phrase. Verse 14 is Deuteronomy 32:36 verbatim. Verses 15 to 18 shorten Psalm 115:4 to 8, with one substitution: Psalm 115 says their idols, this one says the idols of the nations. Verses 19 and 20 take the roll call of Psalm 115:9 to 11, which is also used in Psalm 118, and insert {{20.1}}, the house of Levi, which the other lists do not have. Which text borrowed from which is disputed. Two smaller points for a reader with the Hebrew in front of them: {{7.1}} comes from the root meaning to lift, so the clouds are literally the lifted things, and the lamed on {{11.0}} marks the object of the killing rather than direction, which is why the English has no preposition there. And {{17.5}} with {{17.6}} is a doubled construction, there is not there is, an emphatic that no smooth translation preserves.

Two readings the text sets up on its own. First, the list at the end. Israel, Aaron, Levi are all defined by birth, and then the fourth group is defined by fear of heaven and by nothing else, so the sequence moves from lineage to disposition and closes on the category that anyone can enter. That the widening is deliberate is visible in the structure, since Levi had to be inserted into an existing three part list to make room for it. Second, {{18.2}}, their makers. Read strictly the verse says that the craftsmen come to resemble their product, and the second clause extends the same fate to anyone who merely trusts it, which makes the psalm's target the worshipper rather than the statue. Taken together with verse 17, where the failure of the idol is that no breath comes out of its mouth, the passage measures gods by whether anything speaks.

Breath is the hinge of the mystical reading. The idol has a mouth and no wind in it, while the God of this psalm keeps wind in storehouses and lets it out, and the human being who says these words is doing with breath the one thing the idol cannot do. The praise is therefore not decoration on top of the theology but the demonstration of it: a mouth that produces speech is the evidence being offered. Alongside that, {{4.6}} names Israel as a set apart possession, a term used for treasure kept back from the general stock, and the kabbalistic reading takes it as a description of a portion held in reserve rather than a reward for merit. The psalm then ends by sending the blessing back up from Zion, which is the standard image of a circuit: what descends as rain and history returns as speech.
